years.title: On the threshold of the Age of Discovery
power: After taking Constantinople in 1453, the Ottoman Empire controlled the Balkans and the eastern Mediterranean, holding the chokepoint of the trade routes between Europe and Asia.

Ming China stood at the centre of the East Asian tributary order, but after Zheng He's voyages ended in 1433 it gave up state-run ocean voyages and also kept private seafaring shut out under its maritime ban (haijin).[^haijin]
Portugal worked its way down the West African coast, and in 1488 Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope, opening the way to the Indian Ocean.
Castile and Aragon were joined by the marriage alliance of 1469, and in 1492 they conquered Granada, completing the Reconquista.

events.g: Ottomans — a new imperial capital and the gateway between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean
events.l: End of the Byzantine Empire; Venice and Genoa's eastern trade shrinks

events.g: Castile and Aragon — the basis of Iberian unity, and resources to spare for Atlantic ventures
events.l: The Nasrid dynasty, the last Muslim state in Iberia, disappears

events.g: Castile — claims to lands across the Atlantic
events.l: Indigenous Americans — their numbers later collapse through conquest and epidemics

tech: The caravel and celestial navigation (astrolabe, quadrant): ships that could sail against the wind, and a way to measure latitude, made ocean voyages possible.
Movable-type printing (Gutenberg, 1450s): knowledge, maps and navigational information spread quickly.
Large siege guns broke the walls of Constantinople, showing that the age of the medieval city wall was over.
ideas: Renaissance humanism: Byzantine scholars moving to Italy gave new life to the study of Greek classics.
Religious unity under the Catholic Monarchs: the Alhambra Decree of 1492 expelled Spain's Jews.
Ming neo-Confucian order: a hierarchical view of the world with China at its centre (the tributary system).

years.title: Charles V and Suleiman
power: The Habsburg Charles V (king of Spain 1516, Holy Roman Emperor 1519) ruled Spain, the Netherlands, southern Italy and the New World at once. The Austrian lands were left to his brother Ferdinand.
Francis I of France fought the Italian Wars to break the Habsburg encirclement, and even allied with the Muslim Ottomans (agreement of 1536[^fr_ot]).
The Ottoman sultan Suleiman I crushed Hungary at Mohács in 1526 and besieged Vienna in 1529.
Portugal built a maritime spice empire in the Indian Ocean around bases at Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515).

events.g: Spain and Portugal — divide the non-European world along a meridian (Brazil falls to Portugal)
events.l: Other European states are shut out and later push back; indigenous rights are not considered

events.g: Spain — the lands and silver of the Mexican plateau
events.l: The Aztec empire falls[^inca]

events.g: Charles V — the upper hand in Italy
events.l: Francis I is taken prisoner

events.g: Ottomans — Hungary drawn into their sphere (direct rule over the centre began only with the capture of Buda in 1541). The Habsburgs inherit the crowns of Hungary and Bohemia
events.l: Kingdom of Hungary (Louis II died during the retreat)

tech: Magellan–Elcano circumnavigation (1519–22): proof that the world's oceans are one connected sea.
The Columbian Exchange: maize, potatoes and chillies went to the Old World; horses, wheat and germs went to the New.
Infantry combining arquebuses and pikes, and star-shaped Italian-style fortresses that could withstand cannon.
ideas: The Reformation (Luther's 95 Theses, 1517): carried by print, it split even the politics of the Holy Roman Empire.
Machiavelli's The Prince (published 1532): a science of power separated from morality.
Thomas More's Utopia (1516): an ideal society used to criticise his own times.

years.title: The age of silver and the new sea powers
power: In 1580 Spain also took the Portuguese crown (Iberian Union, to 1640), becoming the most extensive overseas empire of its day, yet it suffered fiscal crises and repeated bankruptcies.
The Netherlands declared independence from Spain in 1581 and rose as a commercial power even while fighting the Eighty Years' War.
England under Elizabeth I defeated the Armada in 1588 and began expanding overseas in earnest.
In East Asia the Imjin War (1592–98) shook Ming China, Joseon Korea and Japan alike, and the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 opened the way to the Tokugawa shogunate.

events.g: Spain — the Andean lands and the Potosí silver mine (found 1545)
events.l: The Inca empire falls (the last resistance at Vilcabamba held out until 1572)

events.g: The Holy League (Spain, Venice, the Papal States) — defends the western Mediterranean
events.l: The Ottoman fleet is destroyed (but rebuilt the next year)[^lepanto]

events.g: England and the Netherlands — confidence at sea, a push into the Atlantic
events.l: The prestige of the Spanish navy

events.g: No clear winner — the Tokugawa house fills the vacuum left by the Toyotomi regime
events.l: Joseon's land is devastated. Ming finances are drained → room for the Jurchens (Later Jin) to rise. The Toyotomi regime is weakened

events.g: English merchants — a charter monopoly on Asian trade
events.l: (In the long run) Portugal's monopoly in the Indian Ocean

tech: Silver goes global: Potosí's mines and mercury amalgamation, plus the Manila galleons (from 1565), sent American silver to China.
Muskets and navies: Japan fielded matchlocks (introduced 1543) in large numbers, while Joseon held the sea with panokseon warships and turtle ships.
The Mercator projection (1569) became the standard for nautical charts.
ideas: The dawn of the Scientific Revolution: Copernicus's heliocentrism (1543) spread; Bruno was burned as a heretic in 1600.
The Counter-Reformation: the Council of Trent (1545–63) and Jesuit missions in Asia (Matteo Ricci).
Sovereignty and toleration: Bodin's Six Books of the Commonwealth (1576) and the Edict of Nantes (1598).

years.title: The Westphalian order and the Dutch Golden Age
power: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) ended the Thirty Years' War. Dutch and Swiss independence was recognised, and it is commonly described as the prototype of a system of coexisting territorial sovereign states.[^westphalia]
The Netherlands, led by the Dutch East India Company (VOC), became the main player in Asian maritime trade.
Spain's decline became obvious when Portugal regained independence in 1640, and France moved to fill the gap (later sealed by the Treaty of the Pyrenees, 1659).
England executed Charles I in 1649 after its civil wars (1642–51) and became a republic. In East Asia the Ming fell in 1644 and the Qing entered Beijing.

events.t: 1618–48 Thirty Years' War / Peace of Westphalia
events.g: France and Sweden (territory), the Netherlands (independence recognised), German princes (de facto sovereignty)
events.l: The emperor's power weakens; the population of the German lands falls sharply

events.g: Portugal — independence regained
events.l: Spain

events.t: 1636–37 Qing invasion of Joseon · 1644 Fall of the Ming
events.g: Qing — subdues Joseon and becomes master of China
events.l: Ming. Joseon becomes a Qing tributary

events.g: English shipping
events.l: Dutch carrying trade → seeds of the Anglo-Dutch Wars (from 1652)

tech: Financial innovation: the VOC (1602) issued shares, and the Amsterdam stock exchange and banks gathered capital.
The fluyt: a Dutch merchant ship that carried large cargoes with a small crew, cutting freight costs.
The telescope (1608) and Galileo's observations (1610), and Gustavus Adolphus's mobile artillery and linear tactics (the military revolution).
ideas: Grotius, On the Law of War and Peace (1625): the starting point of modern international law.
Hobbes, Leviathan (1651): a sovereign state to end the war of all against all.
Descartes, Discourse on the Method (1637): rationalism. The trial of Galileo (1633), by contrast, showed the clash with church authority.

years.title: The Sun King and shifting power in Eastern Europe
power: Louis XIV's France, with the largest army in Europe, was the leading candidate for hegemony.
The Glorious Revolution of 1688 put William of Orange on the English throne, binding the two sea powers into an anti-French alliance.
After failing to take Vienna in 1683, the Ottomans gave up large territories for the first time at the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699.

In Russia, Peter the Great began his Westernising reforms and went to war with Sweden in 1700 (the Great Northern War). Qing China under the Kangxi Emperor fixed its border with Russia in the Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689).

events.t: 1683 Failed siege of Vienna → 1699 Treaty of Karlowitz
events.g: The Habsburgs (Hungary, Transylvania), Poland, Venice
events.l: Ottomans — expansion into Europe ends and the retreat begins

events.g: The English Parliament — Bill of Rights (1689); an Anglo-Dutch partnership
events.l: James II and his pro-French line

events.g: Qing — secures the Amur basin / Russia — a trade route
events.l: (A compromise) Russia's advance on the Amur halts

events.t: 1700 Death of Charles II of Spain
events.g: Louis XIV's grandson Philip is named heir
events.l: A threat to the European balance → War of the Spanish Succession (from 1701)

tech: Newton's Principia (1687): one set of laws for motion in the heavens and on earth.
The fiscal-military state: the Bank of England (1694) and national debt let states pay for long wars.
The flintlock musket with a bayonet became the infantry standard, and Savery's steam pump appeared in 1698.
ideas: Locke, Two Treatises of Government (1689): government by consent to protect life, liberty and property, and the right of resistance.
A culture of experiment and open verification, represented by the Royal Society (1660).
Absolutism and religion: when the Edict of Nantes was revoked in 1685, Huguenot craftsmen left for the Netherlands, England and Prussia.

years.title: Utrecht: the balance of power becomes a rule
power: The War of the Spanish Succession (1701–14) ended with the treaties of Utrecht (1713) and Rastatt (1714). The Bourbon Philip V was recognised as king of Spain, but the French and Spanish crowns could never be united.
England and Scotland united as Great Britain in 1707 and became the war's biggest winner.
Austria gained the Spanish Netherlands, Milan and Naples, becoming a great power in central Europe.
Louis XIV's death in 1715 also ended France's bid for sole hegemony.

events.g: Britain — Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and the right to supply slaves to Spanish America (asiento)
events.l: Spain (its European possessions), France (part of North America)

events.g: Austria — the southern Netherlands, Milan, Naples
events.l: Spain

events.g: Russia — access to the Baltic (Treaty of Nystad, 1721)
events.l: Sweden — loses its status as the great power of the north

tech: Newcomen's atmospheric steam engine (1712): used to drain coal mines, it opened the way to more coal.
Darby's coke smelting (1709): iron melted with coal instead of charcoal.
The Longitude Act (1714): a prize for finding longitude at sea, which led to Harrison's chronometer.
ideas: The balance of power: the principle of blocking any single country's hegemony was written into treaty texts.
The early Enlightenment: Bayle's scepticism and the popularisation of Newtonian science.
Mercantilism: an economic outlook that saw colonies, trade surpluses and naval power as the core of national strength.

years.title: American independence and the collapse of Britain's first empire
power: Britain won the Seven Years' War (1756–63), gaining Canada in the Treaty of Paris (1763) and beating France in India too.
France backed the American War of Independence to take revenge, and the Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognised the United States.
In India, the British East India Company turned into a territorial ruler after the Battle of Plassey (1757) and gaining the tax rights (diwani) of Bengal in 1765.
Russia joined the partition of Poland in 1772 and annexed the Crimean Khanate in 1783, reaching the Black Sea.

events.g: Britain — Canada, Florida, dominance in India / Prussia — keeps Silesia
events.l: France — loses most of its North American colonies

events.g: USA — independence. France and Spain — revenge; Spain regains Florida and Minorca
events.l: Britain — the Thirteen Colonies. France runs up huge war debts, one cause of the Revolution of 1789

events.g: Russia, Prussia, Austria
events.l: Poland–Lithuania

events.g: Russia — the Black Sea coast
events.l: Ottomans — another retreat after the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (1774)

tech: The start of Britain's Industrial Revolution: Hargreaves's spinning jenny (1760s), Arkwright's water frame (1769), Watt's improved steam engine (patent 1769, in use 1776).
Harrison's chronometer (sea trial 1761): longitude could now be measured at sea.
The Montgolfier brothers' hot-air balloon (1783).
ideas: The Enlightenment: Montesquieu's separation of powers in The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762).
Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776): a critique of mercantilism, and the division of labour and markets.
The US Declaration of Independence (1776): natural rights and the consent of the governed. In Korea, Northern Learning (Bukhak) scholars under King Jeongjo argued for adopting Qing technology.

years.title: The Vienna system and British sea power
power: Waterloo (1815) ended the Napoleonic Wars, and the Congress of Vienna redrew Europe on the principles of legitimacy and the balance of power (the Concert of Europe of five great powers).
After Trafalgar (1805) Britain monopolised the seas, gaining maritime bases such as the Cape, Ceylon and Malta.
Russia took Finland (1809) and most of Poland (Congress Poland); Prussia gained the Rhineland.
With Spain itself occupied by Napoleon, wars of independence spread across Latin America.

events.g: USA — roughly doubles its territory
events.l: France — gives up its North American dream to fund the war

events.g: Haiti — the first Black republic
events.l: France — its richest sugar colony

events.t: 1806 Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire
events.g: Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine
events.l: The Habsburg imperial title (becomes Emperor of Austria)

events.g: Britain, Russia, Prussia, Austria
events.l: France — cut back to roughly its 1790 borders. Polish and Italian hopes of national unity are ignored

tech: Citizen armies and conscription (levée en masse, 1793): the scale of war changed.
Steam spreads: Fulton's steamboat (1807), Trevithick's steam locomotive (1804).
Volta's battery (1800), Jenner's smallpox vaccination (1796).
ideas: The French Revolution's Declaration of the Rights of Man (1789) and the Napoleonic Code (1804) spread equality before the law across Europe.
Nationalism: resistance to French occupation (Fichte's Addresses to the German Nation).
Conservatism: Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) and the legitimism of the Vienna system.

years.title: Pax Britannica and the rising powers
power: Britain was the 'workshop of the world' and its financial centre. In 1877 Queen Victoria became Empress of India.
Germany, unified in 1871, isolated France through Bismarck's alliance diplomacy. Defeated France turned to overseas colonies.
Russia pushed south into Central Asia, playing the 'Great Game' against Britain.
The USA industrialised rapidly after the Civil War (1861–65), and Japan modernised after the Meiji Restoration (1868). Most of inland Africa was still outside direct European rule (grey on the map).

events.g: Britain — Hong Kong, treaty ports, tariff privileges
events.l: Qing — drawn into the unequal treaty system

events.t: 1858 Treaty of Aigun · 1860 Convention of Peking
events.g: Russia — land north of the Amur and the Maritime Province (Vladivostok founded)
events.l: Qing

events.g: Germany — unification and Alsace-Lorraine
events.l: France — territory and an indemnity; the Second Empire collapses

events.g: Japan — opens Korea's ports, extraterritoriality
events.l: Joseon — an unequal treaty

events.g: Austria (administers Bosnia), Britain (Cyprus). Serbia, Romania and Montenegro independent
events.l: Russia (gains from the Treaty of San Stefano reduced), Ottomans

tech: Transport and communication revolution: railways, steamships, the transatlantic telegraph cable (1866), the Suez Canal (1869).
The Second Industrial Revolution: Bessemer steel (1856), electricity (Edison's light bulb, 1879), the chemical industry.
Tools of empire: breech-loading rifles and quinine (against malaria) gave Europeans the means to enter inland Africa.
ideas: Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) → distorted into Social Darwinism to justify imperialism.
Marx and Engels, The Communist Manifesto (1848) and Capital (1867).

Nationalism triumphs (Italian and German unification), and East Asia debates how to adopt Western ways (the Self-Strengthening Movement, Japan's 'civilisation and enlightenment', Korea's 'Eastern ways, Western machines').

years.title: The height of imperialism and the outbreak of war
power: After the Berlin Conference (1884–85) the partition of Africa was almost complete; only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

Britain answered Germany's naval build-up with the Dreadnought (1906). Europe split into the Triple Entente (Britain, France, Russia) and the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) — though Italy stayed neutral at the outbreak and joined the Entente side in 1915.
The USA gained the Philippines, Guam and Puerto Rico in the Spanish–American War of 1898.
Japan won the Sino-Japanese (1894–95) and Russo-Japanese (1904–05) wars and annexed Korea in 1910. In China the 1911 Revolution brought down the Qing (Republic of China, 1912).

events.g: USA — Pacific and Caribbean colonies
events.l: Spain — the last of its overseas empire

events.g: Britain — the gold and diamond fields of southern Africa
events.l: The Transvaal and the Orange Free State

events.g: Japan — control over Korea, rights in southern Manchuria
events.l: Russia — its Far Eastern push fails; Revolution of 1905

events.g: Japan
events.l: The Korean Empire
The alliance system turns a local conflict into a world war

tech: The internal combustion engine: the Ford Model T (1908) and the moving assembly line (1913), the Wright brothers' powered flight (1903).
Wireless telegraphy (Marconi, transatlantic transmission 1901) and dreadnought battleships.
The Haber–Bosch process (developed 1909, industrialised 1913): fertiliser and explosives made from nitrogen in the air.
ideas: The 'civilising mission' and racism were used to justify colonial rule.
Socialist parties and the Second International grew, but when war came most of them backed their own governments.

Nationalism in colonies and semi-colonies: Korea's Patriotic Enlightenment Movement, China's Three Principles of the People (Sun Yat-sen), Budi Utomo (1908) and Sarekat Islam in the Dutch East Indies.

years.title: The Versailles system
power: The First World War brought down four empires: Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia and the Ottoman Empire.
Britain and France divided the former German and Ottoman lands in the Middle East and Africa under the name of 'mandates'. The British Empire was at its largest around this time.[^gb_peak]
The USA became the largest creditor nation, but the Senate did not ratify the Treaty of Versailles, so it never joined the League of Nations.
After the 1917 revolution Russia was in civil war (to 1922). Japan gained rights in Shandong and the South Seas islands.

events.g: Germany (temporarily)
events.l: Russia — western lands including Poland, the Baltics and Ukraine

events.g: France (Alsace-Lorraine), Britain and France (mandates), Japan (Shandong, South Seas islands), Poland restored
events.l: Germany — about 13% of its home territory, all its colonies, and huge reparations

events.t: 1919 Treaty of Saint-Germain · 1920 Treaty of Trianon
events.g: New or enlarged states such as Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and Romania
events.l: Austria and Hungary — most of their territory

events.g: National movements go mass (the Korean Provisional Government is founded)
events.l: Disappointment that Wilson's self-determination applied only to the losers' colonies

tech: Technologies of total war: machine guns, tanks, aircraft, submarines, poison gas.
Regular radio broadcasting (KDKA, 1920): the age of mass media began.
Einstein's general relativity (1915) was confirmed by eclipse observations in 1919.
ideas: Wilson's Fourteen Points and self-determination, and collective security through the League of Nations.
Bolshevism and the Comintern (1919): an alternative order calling for world revolution.
Colonial nationalism spreads: Gandhi's Non-cooperation Movement in India (1920).

years.title: The Great Depression and the expansion of fascism
power: The Great Depression of 1929 broke the free-trade order, and economic blocs and militarism gained ground.
Nazi Germany rearmed (1935) and remilitarised the Rhineland (1936), then annexed Austria in March 1938 and took the Sudetenland through the Munich Agreement in September.
Japan launched the Manchurian Incident (1931), set up Manchukuo (1932) and started the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937). Italy conquered Ethiopia in 1935–36.
The USSR industrialised through its Five-Year Plans; the USA answered with the New Deal and isolationism, Britain and France with appeasement.

events.t: 1931 Manchurian Incident · 1933 withdrawal from the League
events.g: Japan — Manchuria (Manchukuo)
events.l: China; trust in the League's collective security

events.g: Italy
events.l: Ethiopia; the League's economic sanctions fail

events.g: Franco (backed by Germany and Italy) — a testing ground for new weapons
events.l: The Spanish Republic

events.g: Germany — Austria, the Sudetenland
events.l: Austria, Czechoslovakia; the limits of British and French appeasement

tech: Radar (British experiment, 1935), the first jet-engine test run (Whittle, 1937).
Nuclear fission discovered in December 1938 (Hahn and Strassmann; theoretical explanation by Meitner and Frisch).
Aircraft carriers and armoured divisions prepared mobile warfare; synthetic materials such as nylon (1935) appeared.
ideas: Fascism and Nazism: totalitarianism, racism, the logic of Lebensraum ('living space').
Stalinism: socialism in one country, the planned economy, the Great Purge.
Keynes's General Theory (1936): government spending in a slump. Non-violent anti-colonial movements such as Gandhi's Salt March (1930).

years.title: The end of the Second World War and the start of a bipolar world
power: Germany (May) and Japan (surrender announced 15 August, signed 2 September) surrendered. The USA held a monopoly on nuclear weapons and was the only great power with overwhelming industrial strength.
The USSR suffered enormous losses of life but occupied all of Eastern Europe and made it its sphere of influence.
Britain and France were among the victors, but their finances were exhausted and they were losing the strength to keep their colonies.

Korea was liberated and at once divided at the 38th parallel between US and Soviet occupation. The United Nations (October 1945) and the Bretton Woods system (IMF, World Bank) became the framework of the post-war order.

events.g: USSR — southern Sakhalin and the Kurils for entering the war against Japan, influence over Eastern Europe
events.l: Self-determination for Poland and Eastern Europe

events.t: 1945.8 Atomic bombs · Soviet entry into the war · Japan surrenders
events.g: USA — sole occupation of Japan. Korea liberated; China recovers Taiwan and Manchuria
events.l: Japan — all its colonies and occupied lands

events.g: Indonesia — declares independence
events.l: The Netherlands — tries to return; transfers sovereignty in 1949 after the war of independence

events.g: The USA, Britain, France and the USSR
events.l: Germany — lands east of the Oder–Neisse line

tech: The atomic bomb (Manhattan Project), radar and the proximity fuze.
Jet aircraft (Me 262) and the V-2 ballistic missile — after the war the USA and USSR raced to recruit German engineers.
Mass-produced penicillin and electronic computers (Colossus, ENIAC).
ideas: The UN Charter: sovereign equality, the ban on the use of force, collective security.
Once the anti-fascist alliance ended, the confrontation between liberal democracy and communism began.
The welfare state (Beveridge Report, 1942) and Keynesianism, and an explosion of colonial demands for self-determination.

years.title: The Cold War and the year of decolonisation
power: NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955) hardened the two blocs.
The People's Republic of China was founded in 1949, and the Korean War (1950–53) froze the division of East Asia.
In the Suez Crisis of 1956 Britain and France backed down under US and Soviet pressure, confirming that the age of the old empires was over.
1960 was the 'Year of Africa', when 17 countries became independent. In the same year the USSR pulled its experts out of China, exposing the Sino-Soviet split.

events.t: 1947 Independence and partition of India and Pakistan
events.g: India and Pakistan
events.l: Britain — the heart of its empire. Partition brought mass refugee flows and massacres

events.t: 1949 End of the Chinese Civil War
events.g: The Chinese Communist Party
events.l: The Nationalists — move to Taiwan

events.g: The Viet Minh
events.l: France — Indochina

events.g: Egypt (nationalises the canal), the voice of the USA and USSR
events.l: The prestige of Britain and France

tech: Sputnik (1957) and ICBMs: the age of the space race and nuclear deterrence.
Hydrogen bombs (USA 1952, USSR 1953 and 1955).
The transistor (1947) and the integrated circuit (1958–59); the double-helix structure of DNA (1953).
ideas: The Bandung Conference (1955) and the Non-Aligned Movement: a 'Third World' belonging to neither bloc.
UN General Assembly Resolution 1514 (1960): the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples.
The US civil rights movement, and the systemic contest between Marxism-Leninism and liberal democracy.

years.title: The end of the Cold War and a unipolar America
power: The Berlin Wall fell in 1989, Germany reunified in 1990, and the Soviet Union dissolved into 15 republics in 1991.
The USA showed its military and diplomatic superiority in the 1991 Gulf War and became the sole superpower.
Europe launched the EU with the Maastricht Treaty (signed 1992, in force November 1993).
After 'reform and opening up' in 1978, China accelerated its turn to a market economy with Deng Xiaoping's Southern Tour in 1992.

events.g: West Germany (Federal Republic)
events.l: The East German regime disappears; Soviet influence in central Europe

events.g: US-led coalition — Kuwait restored, the power of precision weapons on display
events.l: Iraq

events.g: Newly independent states, the Western bloc
events.l: Russia — territory, population and allies sharply reduced; economic collapse

events.t: 1991 Both Koreas join the UN · 1994 South Africa's first all-race election
events.g: International recognition of two Korean states / South Africa's Black majority
events.l: The apartheid regime

tech: The World Wide Web (1991) and the spread of personal computers.
GPS (initial operation 1993) and precision-guided weapons.
2G digital mobile communications (GSM, 1991).
ideas: Neoliberalism and the 'Washington Consensus': privatisation, deregulation, trade liberalisation.
The debate between Fukuyama's 'End of History' (1989 essay) and Huntington's 'Clash of Civilizations' (1993 essay).
Globalisation and regional integration (the EU launched, NAFTA 1994).

years.title: US–China rivalry and signs of a multipolar world
power: After the 9/11 attacks in 2001 the USA fought long wars in Afghanistan (2001) and Iraq (2003).
The 2008 global financial crisis made the G20 summit a central forum.
After joining the WTO in 2001 China became the 'workshop of the world', and in 2010 it passed Japan to become the world's second-largest economy by nominal GDP.
Russia's 2008 war with Georgia showed its determination to regain influence in the former Soviet space.

events.g: China — export-led growth
events.l: Some manufacturing jobs in developed countries (production moves)

events.g: (Short term) the US-led coalition — removes Saddam Hussein's regime
events.l: USA — enormous cost and international trust. Iraq — a long civil war

events.g: Emerging economies' relative voice (G20)
events.l: Trust in the US and European financial systems

events.g: Russia — control of South Ossetia and Abkhazia
events.l: Georgia; plans to enlarge NATO

tech: Smartphones (the iPhone, 2007), social media, 4G LTE.
The shale revolution (horizontal drilling + hydraulic fracturing): a surge in US energy production.
Drone warfare and cyber attacks (Stuxnet discovered in 2010).
ideas: The 'Beijing Consensus' and state capitalism: the rise of an authoritarian growth model.
The war on terror and debates over human rights and sovereignty.
Climate change (Copenhagen conference, 2009), and early signs of anti-globalisation and populism.

notes.haijin: The maritime ban itself was first issued in 1371 under the Hongwu Emperor, and Zheng He's voyages (1405–33) were a state enterprise carried out while private trade stayed banned. After the voyages the Ming did not so much 'close the sea' as stop state-led voyaging. The ban was partly relaxed in 1567.
notes.fr_ot: Only a draft of the 1536 agreement survives, and it is uncertain whether it was formally ratified then (formal ratification is usually dated to 1569). Military cooperation between the two did take place, however. It falls slightly after the 1530 date of this map.
notes.inca: The conquest of the Incas began in 1532, after this date (1530). On this map the Incas are still independent; the conquest is covered under 'Gains and losses' for the next year shown (1600).
notes.lepanto: In the same war the Ottomans took Cyprus (1571) and rebuilt their fleet the following year. How far Lepanto changed the balance in the Mediterranean is debated.
notes.westphalia: The claim that Westphalia created the system of sovereign states has been criticised as an interpretation that hardened in the 19th and 20th centuries (Osiander 2001). The treaties dealt mainly with the internal order of the Holy Roman Empire, and Dutch and Swiss independence was closer to confirming an established fact.
notes.gb_peak: The British Empire's greatest extent is usually dated to the early 1920s. Area figures vary with whether the dominions and mandates are counted. This map colours the dominions as British in 1914 and 1920.
notes.us_ww2: The size of the increase depends on the measure. Nominal GNP more than doubled between 1939 and 1945, but in real terms, adjusted for prices, the rise was smaller.
notes.jp_1968: 1968 is the year Japan's GNP overtook West Germany's, meaning second among Western countries. Depending on estimates of the Soviet economy, the date it became 'second in the world' can be put differently.
notes.goa: Goa was changing hands in this period. Bijapur (the Adil Shahis) broke from the Bahmani Sultanate in 1490, and sources differ on when in the 1490s it took control of Goa. It was Bijapur that Portugal took Goa from in 1510.
notes.aden: The main Tahirid line fell to the Mamluk invasion of 1517. Aden alone was held by the last Tahirid ruler until it passed to the Ottomans in 1538.
notes.crimea: The Crimean Khanate ran its own internal affairs, and how far it was subordinate to the Ottomans is debated among scholars (some see an unequal alliance). This map colours it Ottoman on the basis of control over the strategic points north of the Black Sea.
notes.egypt_1914: On this map's reference date (July 1914) Egypt was nominally Ottoman while occupied and run by Britain since 1882. The protectorate was declared in December that year. It is shown as British on the basis of effective control.

t.1492: Kingdom of England. It lost its lands in France in the Hundred Years' War (ended 1453), and the Tudor dynasty came to power in 1485 after the Wars of the Roses. Still a mid-sized kingdom on Europe's edge.
t.1530: Reign of Henry VIII. Its only continental possession is Calais. Soon, the Act of Supremacy (1534) breaks with Rome → the start of rivalry with Catholic Spain.
t.1600: Elizabeth I defeated the Armada in 1588 → confidence at sea, and the East India Company was founded in 1600 to trade overseas. The conquest of Ireland is under way.
t.1650: Colonies in North America (Jamestown 1607) and the Caribbean. A republic after the civil wars (1642–51). The Navigation Act of 1651 challenges the Dutch carrying trade → Anglo-Dutch Wars.
t.1700: The Glorious Revolution (1688) brought parliamentary sovereignty and public-debt finance (Bank of England, 1694) → the money to sustain long wars and compete with France for hegemony.
t.1715: Union with Scotland as Great Britain (1707). Victory in the War of the Spanish Succession brought Gibraltar, Minorca, North American land and the slave-trade asiento → it rises to sea power.
t.1783: Victory in the Seven Years' War (1756–63) gave it Canada and the upper hand in India, but taxing the colonies to pay for it provoked the American war and the loss of the Thirteen Colonies. Rule in India grew instead, shifting the empire's centre of gravity to Asia.
t.1815: Victory in the Napoleonic Wars. After Trafalgar (1805) it controls the seas, and the Industrial Revolution puts its economy ahead → the start of 'Pax Britannica'.
t.1880: Workshop of the world and financial centre. After the Indian Rebellion (1857) it rules India directly (1858); Victoria becomes Empress of India (1877). But German and US industry begin to catch up.
t.1914: The partition of Africa secures a line from Egypt to South Africa. Facing Germany's naval challenge, it drops 'splendid isolation' and reaches understandings with France and Russia → enters the war.
t.1920: Victory plus mandates make its territory the largest ever. But it owes war debts to the USA, and Ireland's war of independence (hatched) and Indian nationalism grow → the largest on the outside, weakening inside.
t.1938: After the Depression it builds an economic bloc through imperial preference. Fiscal strain and public dread of war lead it to appease Germany.
t.1945: A victor, but close to bankruptcy and dependent on US loans. Indian independence (1947) is near — it is losing the strength to hold the empire.
t.1960: Colonies become independent one after another, beginning with India (1947). Backing down under US pressure in the Suez Crisis (1956) shows its independent exercise of hegemony is over.
t.1994: Decolonisation is almost complete (only Hong Kong, to be returned in 1997). Influence remains as a close US ally and permanent Security Council member, but it has left the contest for hegemony — the state continues.
t.2010: With Hong Kong returned (1997) the overseas empire is effectively over. It keeps great-power status but is not a lead contender for world hegemony.

t.1492: Having driven England out in the Hundred Years' War (ended 1453), the most populous kingdom in Europe. Its invasion of Italy in 1494 brings it into the contest for hegemony.
t.1530: Head-on clash with the Habsburgs (Charles V) in the Italian Wars. Surrounded by Habsburg lands, it allies even with the Muslim Ottomans.
t.1600: Tied down by the Wars of Religion (1562–98), it ends civil war with Henry IV's Edict of Nantes (1598) and begins to rebuild.
t.1650: Wins against the Habsburgs in the Thirty Years' War (Westphalia, 1648) → part of Alsace. Replaces declining Spain as the strongest continental power.
t.1700: Louis XIV's absolute monarchy: Europe's largest army and the colonies of Canada and Louisiana. Trying to put his grandson on the Spanish throne leads to war with a European coalition.
t.1715: War of the Spanish Succession: the grandson keeps the Spanish throne, but the two crowns may never unite, and Newfoundland and Nova Scotia go to Britain.
t.1783: Defeat in the Seven Years' War cost it Canada and the lead in India (1763). Helping American independence brought revenge, but the debts it piled up sparked the Revolution of 1789.
t.1815: Through the Revolution and Napoleon's empire it once ruled most of Europe, but defeat → cut back to roughly its 1790 borders, having also lost Haiti and Louisiana. The country did not fall; the monarchy was restored.
t.1880: After losing Alsace-Lorraine in the Franco-Prussian War (1871), it makes up for it by expanding colonies in Africa (centred on Algeria) and Indochina.
t.1914: The world's second-largest colonial empire, in West and North Africa and Indochina. Allied with Russia and Britain to contain Germany.
t.1920: As a victor it regains Alsace-Lorraine and gets mandates over Syria and Lebanon. But its northern industrial region was a battlefield and the damage is huge.
t.1938: The empire is at its largest, but political instability and a defensive strategy (Maginot Line) lead it to appease German expansion. Defeat and occupation come in 1940.
t.1945: Occupied by Germany 1940–44, then liberated. Treated as a victor, but much weakened, and colonial demands for independence grow.
t.1960: Lost the Indochina War (1954); most African colonies independent (1960). The Algerian War of Independence (hatched) is under way.
t.1994: The colonial empire is gone, but it remains a nuclear power, a permanent Security Council member and a pillar of the EU. State and influence continue; it has left the contest for world hegemony.
t.2010: A core EU member. Only some overseas territories remain.

t.1492: Castile and Aragon were joined under one royal couple by the marriage of 1469, but are still two kingdoms with their own laws and parliaments. They rise with the conquest of Granada and Columbus's voyage in 1492.
t.1530: In 1516 Charles I inherited both crowns together, so it became 'Spain' in practice (a change of name, not a disappearance). As Holy Roman Emperor Charles V from 1519 he also ruled the Netherlands, Naples, Sicily and Sardinia. The conquest of the Aztecs begins the American empire — homeland and colonies share one colour.
t.1600: Charles V's abdication (1556) split the Habsburgs in two: Spain, the Netherlands, Italy and the Americas to his son Philip II, Austria to his brother Ferdinand. Adding the Portuguese crown in 1580 makes it the largest ever. But the northern Netherlands declared independence (1581) and the Armada failed (1588).
t.1650: Defeat in the Thirty Years' War, Portugal's independence (1640) and recognition of Dutch independence (1648) → European hegemony passes to France. The American colonies remain intact.
t.1700: Charles II dies without an heir in 1700 → the Spanish Habsburg line ends. Louis XIV's grandson (Philip V of Bourbon) is named, starting the War of the Spanish Succession.
t.1715: Treaty of Utrecht: in return for recognition of the Bourbon dynasty it gives the southern Netherlands and Italian lands to Austria and Savoy, and Gibraltar and Minorca to Britain. The homeland and the Americas stay — the country did not fall; its influence in Europe shrank.
t.1783: Bourbon reforms reorganise colonial government. Fighting Britain alongside France in the American war, it regains Florida and Minorca → its American empire is at its largest.
t.1815: Napoleon occupies the homeland in 1808 → with the mother country absent, the American colonies begin wars of independence (from 1810). The monarchy is restored in 1814.
t.1880: Most of its mainland American colonies became independent in the 1820s. Only Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, some Pacific islands (Guam and others) and a few footholds in Africa remain.
t.1914: Defeat in the Spanish–American War (1898) → Cuba independent; the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam go to the USA. Only northern Morocco and parts of West Africa remain.
t.1920: Neutral in the First World War. On the eve of the Rif War in northern Morocco (1921–26).
t.1938: Drained by the Civil War (1936–39). Franco's side is closing in on victory.
t.1945: Stayed out of the Second World War. Internationally isolated under Franco's dictatorship.
t.1960: Returned its Moroccan protectorate in 1956. Only Western Sahara, Equatorial Guinea and Ifni (returned 1969) remain.
t.1994: Equatorial Guinea independent (1968) and withdrawal from Western Sahara (1975) end the colonial empire. Democratisation after Franco; joins the European Community in 1986 — the state continues, out of the contest for hegemony.

t.1492: Exploring the West African coast is a national project. In 1488 Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope; the sea route to India is within reach.
t.1530: After da Gama reached India (1498) it seized Goa, Malacca and Hormuz and dominates the Indian Ocean spice trade. Reached Brazil in 1500.
t.1600: Its royal line died out in 1580 and the Spanish king also became king of Portugal (Iberian Union) → it now suffers attacks from Spain's enemies, the Dutch and English. The kingdom itself stays separate.
t.1650: Independence regained in 1640. Meanwhile the Dutch took its Asian bases such as Malacca (1641) → Indian Ocean dominance lost; the empire now centres on Brazil.
t.1700: Gold found in Brazil in the 1690s → Brazil becomes the centre of the empire. Close alliance with England.
t.1715: Sided with Britain in the War of the Spanish Succession. Prospers on Brazilian gold.
t.1783: Pombal's reforms after the Lisbon earthquake (1755). Keeps Brazil, Angola, Mozambique, Goa and more.
t.1815: The court fled Napoleon's invasion to Brazil in 1807 → the relationship between metropole and colony is reversed. This leads to Brazilian independence in 1822.
t.1880: After losing Brazil it reorganises around African colonies such as Angola and Mozambique.
t.1914: Republic proclaimed in 1910. Keeps its African colonies.
t.1920: Fought on the Allied side in the First World War. Keeps its colonies.
t.1938: Salazar's dictatorship (Estado Novo). Binds its colonies as 'overseas territories'.
t.1945: Neutral in the Second World War. Keeps its colonies.
t.1960: Holds on while other European powers give up colonies → the next year it loses Goa to India (1961) and colonial wars begin, starting in Angola.
t.1994: The Carnation Revolution (1974) → all African colonies independent in 1974–75 (East Timor was occupied by Indonesia in 1975). Only Macau remains, due back in 1999. Joined the European Community in 1986.
t.2010: With Macau returned in 1999, the overseas empire is completely over.

t.1600: The seven northern provinces, once Spanish Habsburg lands, declared independence in 1581 → they grow through shipping and finance even while at war (they were not an independent country at earlier points). Just before the VOC is founded (1602).
t.1650: The VOC takes Portuguese bases and reaches the East Indies (Indonesia), Ceylon, Taiwan and northern Brazil. Independence recognised in 1648. The golden age of maritime trade.
t.1700: Worn down by the Anglo-Dutch Wars and France's invasion (1672). William III becomes king of England in 1688, joining with England — but the lead gradually passes to England.
t.1715: The cost of the War of the Spanish Succession empties its treasury → sea power passes to Britain. It remains a centre of trade and finance.
t.1783: Defeat in the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War (1780–84) hurts its shipping. The VOC also declines (dissolved 1799).
t.1815: Occupied by French revolutionary armies (Batavian Republic 1795, then annexed by France). Meanwhile Britain took Ceylon and the Cape → after the Congress of Vienna it returns as a kingdom joined with the south (Belgium) and gets the East Indies back.
t.1880: Belgium broke away in 1830. The Cultivation System (1830–70) in the East Indies brings huge profits.
t.1914: Neutral in the First World War. The Aceh War (1873–1904) completed its control of the whole archipelago.
t.1920: Stays neutral. Nationalism grows in the East Indies.
t.1938: Keeps the East Indies. German occupation comes in 1940.
t.1945: Germany occupied the homeland in 1940 and Japan the East Indies in 1942. Indonesia declared independence in August 1945 → war to retake it (hatched).
t.1960: Sovereignty transferred to Indonesia in 1949. Only West New Guinea (handed over 1962) and Suriname remain.
t.1994: Suriname independent in 1975. Only Caribbean islands remain as constituent countries of the kingdom — out of the contest for hegemony.
t.2010: Only Caribbean islands remain as constituent countries of the kingdom.

t.1492: Grand Duchy of Moscow. Ivan III ended Mongol (Golden Horde) rule in 1480 and is uniting north-eastern Russia.
t.1530: Vasily III annexed Pskov (1510) and Smolensk (1514). Soon Ivan IV takes the title of tsar (1547) and conquers Kazan (1552).
t.1600: After Ivan IV the dynasty died out → the 'Time of Troubles' (1598–1613): civil war and Polish and Swedish invasions. Expansion into Siberia continues even so.
t.1650: Stabilised under the Romanovs (1613). Following the fur trade across Siberia it reached the Pacific in 1639. Eastern Ukraine joins in 1654.
t.1700: The Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689) fixed the border with Qing China. Peter the Great begins Westernising reforms and the Great Northern War with Sweden.
t.1715: Victory at Poltava (1709) opens the Baltic; St Petersburg is built → leads to the proclamation of the Empire in 1721.
t.1783: Catherine II: partition of Poland (1772), the Black Sea coast taken from the Ottomans, Crimea annexed in 1783.
t.1815: Repelled Napoleon's invasion (1812) and marched to Paris. Takes Finland and most of Poland → Europe's strongest land power.
t.1880: Defeat in the Crimean War (1856) blocked the Black Sea, so it turned to Central Asia and the Far East (Maritime Province 1860), playing the 'Great Game' with Britain. Serfs emancipated in 1861.
t.1914: Shaken by defeat by Japan and the Revolution of 1905. Industrialising with French capital and joined the Triple Entente.
t.1920: Revolution in 1917 → the Bolsheviks made a separate peace with Germany in 1918, giving up western lands. Civil war under way. This leads to the USSR in 1922 — the state did not fall; the regime changed.
t.1938: The USSR. Rapid industrialisation through the Five-Year Plans; the Great Purge.
t.1945: Defeating Germany, it occupies Eastern Europe and makes it its sphere of influence. A superpower alongside the USA.
t.1960: Nuclear weapons (1949), Sputnik (1957). Eastern European satellites and the Warsaw Pact. Conflict with China begins.
t.1994: The USSR dissolved in 1991 → the Russian Federation is the successor state. Territory, population and allies shrink sharply; the economy collapses.
t.2010: Recovered through energy exports. The 2008 war with Georgia showed its will to regain influence over the former Soviet space.

t.1492: A rising empire holding the Balkans and Anatolia since conquering Constantinople in 1453.
t.1530: Conquering the Mamluks (1517) brought Egypt, Syria, Mecca and Medina; Hungary was crushed at Mohács (1526). Suleiman I's golden age.
t.1600: Rebuilt its fleet after Lepanto (1571) and kept its lands. But price inflation and military costs strain its finances.
t.1650: Despite internal political turmoil, expansion continues (Cretan War, 1645–69).
t.1700: Failure at Vienna (1683) → the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699) gave up most of Hungary, its first great loss. The end of expansion into Europe.
t.1715: Beat Russia at the Pruth in 1711, but soon lost more land to the Habsburgs (1718).
t.1783: Defeated by Russia (Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca, 1774) → Crimea lost to Russia in 1783.
t.1815: Serbian uprising (from 1804); Muhammad Ali's Egypt de facto independent (from 1805). Just before Greek independence (1830).
t.1880: Despite the Tanzimat reforms it was beaten by Russia (1877–78) → at the Congress of Berlin Serbia, Romania and Montenegro become independent and Bulgaria autonomous. Britain took Cyprus, and soon occupied Egypt as well (1882).
t.1914: The Balkan Wars (1912–13) cost most of its European lands; Libya went to Italy (1912). Enters the war on Germany's side.
t.1920: Defeat → the Allies occupy Istanbul and its Arab lands become British and French mandates. The Treaty of Sèvres threatens partition.
t.1938: Ended: the sultanate was abolished in 1922 and the Republic of Turkey founded in 1923 (Treaty of Lausanne). The empire is gone and Turkey succeeds it in Anatolia — not coloured at later points.

t.1492: Ming. A Han Chinese dynasty that drove out the Mongols, at the centre of the East Asian tributary order. Its maritime ban turned it away from the sea; it concentrates on defending the north against the Mongols.
t.1530: Ming. Pressure from wokou pirates and the Mongols (Altan Khan). The maritime ban continues.
t.1600: Ming. Easing the maritime ban in 1567 lets American silver flow in. Sending troops in the Imjin War (1592–98) drains its finances → an opening for the Jurchens to rise.
t.1650: When the Ming fell to peasant rebellion in 1644, the Manchu Qing entered Beijing → a change of dynasty. The dynasty and ruling class changed, but the state of 'China' continued.
t.1700: Kangxi Emperor: suppressed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories (1681), conquered Taiwan (1683), Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689).
t.1715: The golden age continuing through Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong.
t.1783: The Qianlong Emperor conquered the Dzungars and Xinjiang (1759) — its largest extent.
t.1815: Rapid population growth, official corruption, the White Lotus Rebellion (1796–1804). Opium smuggling begins to spread.
t.1880: Defeats in the Opium Wars (1840, 1856) bring unequal treaties; the Maritime Province is ceded to Russia; the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64).
t.1914: Defeat by Japan (1895) cost Taiwan and suzerainty over Korea. The 1911 Revolution → Republic of China (1912). The warlord era begins.
t.1920: Divided among warlords. May Fourth Movement (1919).
t.1938: Nominally unified by the Nationalist Northern Expedition (1928). Japan took Manchuria (1931) and, in the war from 1937, the east coast.
t.1945: As a victor it recovers Taiwan and Manchuria and gets a permanent Security Council seat. But civil war is about to resume.
t.1960: People's Republic founded in 1949 (Nationalists to Taiwan). Fought in the Korean War; the Great Leap Forward (1958) failed; conflict with the USSR.
t.1994: Reform and opening up (1978) and the Southern Tour (1992) → rapid growth. Hong Kong due back in 1997.
t.2010: Joined the WTO in 2001 → workshop of the world; second-largest economy by GDP in 2010. A rivalry with the USA takes shape.

t.1783: The Thirteen Colonies declared independence in 1776 and, with French and Spanish help, won recognition in 1783 → a new republic reaching the Mississippi (British colonies at earlier points).
t.1815: The Louisiana Purchase (1803) doubled its territory. The War of 1812 with Britain ended without territorial change.
t.1880: The Mexican War (1846–48) secured the West; Alaska bought in 1867. Rapid industrialisation after the Civil War (1861–65).
t.1914: The Spanish–American War (1898) brought the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam; Hawaii annexed. Panama Canal opened in 1914. The world's largest industrial power.
t.1920: Its entry in 1917 decided the war and it became the largest creditor nation. But it stayed out of the League of Nations → retreat into isolationism.
t.1938: The Depression → the New Deal. Neutrality Acts keep it out of European conflicts.
t.1945: Entered the war after Pearl Harbor (1941); war production greatly enlarged the economy.[^us_ww2] Nuclear monopoly and sole occupation of Japan → a superpower.
t.1960: Bound Western Europe through the Marshall Plan and NATO; fought in Korea. Space and nuclear race with the USSR.
t.1994: With the USSR dissolved, the sole superpower. Won the Gulf War.
t.2010: Burdened by the Afghanistan and Iraq wars after 9/11, and by the 2008 financial crisis. Still the strongest power, but China is catching up.

t.1700: Brandenburg-Prussia. Grew into a state built around a standing army after the Thirty Years' War; proclaimed the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701.
t.1715: Joined the anti-French alliance in the War of the Spanish Succession and won recognition as a kingdom. Builds up its army.
t.1783: Frederick the Great: took Silesia from Austria (1742), survived the Seven Years' War, joined the partition of Poland (1772) → one of the five great powers.
t.1815: Crushed by Napoleon in 1806 and stripped of half its lands by the Treaty of Tilsit (1807) → reformed, fought the War of Liberation, and gained the Rhineland at the Congress of Vienna.
t.1880: Bismarck: victories over Denmark (1864), Austria (1866) and France (1870–71) → German Empire unified in 1871. Industrial output catches up with Britain.
t.1914: The world's second industrial power. Colonies in Africa and the Pacific. A naval race with Britain ends in war.
t.1920: Defeat and revolution bring down the empire; the Weimar Republic. The Treaty of Versailles takes 13% of its home territory, all colonies, and imposes reparations.
t.1938: Nazi Germany: rearmament; in 1938 the annexation of Austria and the Sudetenland.
t.1945: Ended (temporarily): unconditional surrender dissolves the government and four powers divide and occupy it. Lands east of the Oder–Neisse lost.
t.1960: Rebuilt in 1949 as two states, West and East Germany. The West: economic miracle and NATO; the East: Warsaw Pact — not a contender for hegemony.
t.1994: Reunified in 1990. The central economy of the EU.
t.2010: Europe's largest economy. Keeps its distance from military rivalry.

t.1530: Habsburg Austria. Ruled by Charles V's brother Ferdinand, who inherited the crowns of Bohemia and Hungary in 1526. Held off the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1529. (In the source map it is folded into the Holy Roman Empire and cannot be coloured separately)
t.1600: After the Habsburg split in 1556, the Austrian line holds the imperial title and Austria, Bohemia and western Hungary. Long war with the Ottomans (1593–1606). (Folded into the Holy Roman Empire on the map)
t.1650: The Thirty Years' War (1618–48) weakened imperial power, but its hereditary lands remain.
t.1700: After repelling the siege of Vienna (1683) it counter-attacked → Hungary and Transylvania gained in the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699).
t.1715: The War of the Spanish Succession brings it the Spanish Netherlands, Milan, Naples and Sardinia — its largest extent in central Europe.
t.1783: Lost Silesia to Prussia (1742). Reforms of Maria Theresa and Joseph II; Galicia gained in the partition of Poland.
t.1815: Repeatedly beaten by Napoleon; the Holy Roman Empire dissolved in 1806. At the Congress of Vienna (Metternich) it gains Lombardy–Venetia and presides over the German Confederation.
t.1880: Lost in Italian unification and the war with Prussia (1866), pushed out of German affairs → Austria-Hungary dual monarchy (1867). Administers Bosnia from 1878.
t.1914: National conflicts in a multinational empire. Annexing Bosnia (1908) → the Sarajevo assassination (1914) sets off the war.
t.1920: Ended: dissolved with defeat in 1918 → split into Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and more. The remaining Austrian republic is a small country (annexed by Germany in 1938).

t.1880: The Meiji Restoration (1868) → Western-style modernisation and conscription. Opened Korea with the Treaty of Ganghwa (1876); annexed Ryukyu (1879).
t.1914: Won the Sino-Japanese War (1895: Taiwan) and the Russo-Japanese War (1905: southern Sakhalin, rights in southern Manchuria); annexed Korea in 1910. Anglo-Japanese Alliance (1902).
t.1920: On the Allied side in the First World War → rights in Shandong and the South Seas islands. Permanent member of the League Council.
t.1938: Manchurian Incident (1931), Manchukuo (1932), left the League (1933), war with China (1937) → expanding into East Asia.
t.1945: Empire ended: defeat cost all its colonies and occupied lands, and the USA occupied it (1945–52). The state remained and regained sovereignty in 1952.
t.1960: Sovereignty regained in 1952. Economic recovery under the US–Japan Security Treaty — out of the military contest for hegemony.
t.1994: The world's second-largest economy (from 1968).[^jp_1968] Long stagnation after the bubble burst (1991).
t.2010: Overtaken by China in GDP in 2010, falling to third.

t.1880: Kingdom of Italy proclaimed in 1861; unification completed by taking Rome in 1870. The youngest great power.
t.1914: Eritrea and Somalia, then Libya in 1912. A member of the Triple Alliance, but entered the war on the Entente side in 1915.
t.1920: A victor that did not get all the land it wanted — resentment over a 'mutilated victory' → the rise of fascism (Mussolini in power 1922).
t.1938: Fascist Italy: conquered Ethiopia in 1936; the Axis with Germany.
t.1945: Surrender and civil war from 1943 → a defeated power. Republic in 1946; under the 1947 peace treaty it renounced all its colonies (only former Italian Somaliland was entrusted to it as a UN trusteeship, 1950–60) — the state continues, out of the contest for hegemony.
t.1960: Founding member of NATO and the European Economic Community. Economic miracle.

t.1914: Independent from the Netherlands in 1830. Leopold II's private Congo Free State (1885) became the Belgian Congo in 1908 after atrocities. Invaded by Germany in 1914.
t.1920: A victor. Mandate over part of former German East Africa (Ruanda-Urundi).
t.1945: Occupied by Germany 1940–44, then liberated. Congo's resources (uranium and more) supplied the Allies.
t.1960: Congo independent in 1960 → the Congo Crisis follows at once. Rwanda and Burundi due to become independent in 1962.
t.1994: No colonies. Host of EU and NATO headquarters.

t.1530: In 1526 Babur defeated the Delhi Sultanate at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire.
t.1600: Akbar: unified most of northern India; a policy of religious tolerance.
t.1650: Shah Jahan: built the Taj Mahal; the empire prospers.
t.1700: Aurangzeb conquered the Deccan — the largest extent. But endless wars and religious repression bring more revolts.
t.1715: Succession struggles after Aurangzeb's death (1707) → the Marathas and provincial governors become effectively independent.
t.1783: Nader Shah sacked Delhi (1739); after Plassey (1757) the British East India Company controls Bengal. The emperor exists in name only.
t.1815: The British East India Company took Delhi in 1803 → the emperor is a symbolic figure living on a Company pension.
t.1880: Ended: after the failed Indian Rebellion of 1857, Britain deposed the last emperor (1858) and ruled India directly.
